name: Prize crossword No 25,167
preamble: Half the clues work thus: "Constructed criminality" would lead to BUILT/GUILT, "Liquid grinder" to MILK/MILL and "Life-changing river" to FILE/NILE. Either may be the correct solution to enter in the grid, but the 26 squares of the perimeter need to contain all the letters of the alphabet, which will determine the correct one to be entered.

clue.text: Student comes in about teatime with a showy gesture

indicators.note: something that comes in enters a space, so one piece goes inside the other

blocks.note: L is the learner driver's plate, standard for a student
four o'clock is the traditional hour for afternoon tea
-ish added to a time means roughly that time

explanation.surface: A student makes a grand entrance around four o'clock, waving theatrically.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About teatime' is FOUR-ISH, the casual way of saying roughly four o'clock; the student's L goes inside it after the F.
explanation.definitionFit: A flourish is a bold, sweeping movement made to draw attention, such as a wave of the hand.

blocks.note: first word: to unite or bind together
second word defines UNIT, the partner that differs by one letter, as the preamble describes

explanation.walkthrough: Per the preamble, each word defines one of a pair differing by one letter: KNIT and UNIT. The perimeter needs K (U appears elsewhere at the edge), so KNIT goes in.
explanation.definitionFit: To knit is to grow or bind together firmly, as broken bones mend and fuse.

blocks.note: first word defines YELLOW, the partner word one letter away, as the preamble describes
second word: a loud deep shout

explanation.walkthrough: The pair is YELLOW (cowardly) and BELLOW (cry). Y is already on the perimeter at the foot of 21, while B is needed, so BELLOW is entered.
explanation.definitionFit: To bellow is to shout or roar loudly, like a bull, which is one kind of cry.

blocks.note: first part: to credit something to a cause or person
second part: the letters of 'sic beer', not in that order, give ESCRIBE, the partner word one letter away

explanation.walkthrough: Here the partner is clued by wordplay: 'sic' plus 'beer' rearranged makes ESCRIBE, a geometry verb for drawing a circle touching one side of a triangle. E is already on the perimeter (end of 14), so A is needed.
explanation.definitionFit: To ascribe something is to credit or assign it to a particular source, cause or author.

blocks.note: first word defines PUNCTURE, a flat tyre, the partner word one letter away
second word: a particular moment or stage, as in 'at this point'

explanation.walkthrough: A flat is a punctured tyre. PUNCTURE and JUNCTURE differ only in the first letter; P is already on the perimeter (top of 7), and J appears nowhere else, so JUNCTURE goes in.
explanation.definitionFit: A juncture is a particular moment in time or a critical stage in events, much like a point.

blocks.note: first part defines RESPONDENT, the party against whom a divorce petition is brought, the partner word one letter away
second word: low in spirits

explanation.walkthrough: In a divorce case the spouse being sued is the respondent; 'maybe' marks it as one example. R is already on the perimeter (end of 11), so the D version is entered.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who feels down is dejected and gloomy, having lost hope or heart.

blocks.note: first word: plain to see, obvious
second word defines LATENT, hidden or dormant, the partner word one letter away

explanation.walkthrough: The two words are opposites, and so are the pair PATENT and LATENT. L is already on the perimeter (end of 22 across), so P is needed here.
explanation.definitionFit: Patent in its adjective sense means obvious or evident, as in 'a patent lie' that anyone can see through.

blocks.note: first part: a contagious bacterial infection of horses and donkeys
second part defines FLANDERS, the Flemish region of Belgium, the partner word one letter away

explanation.surface: A vet reports an equine illness found in Belgium.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as one disease located in one country; in fact the last two words define a separate region. F is already on the perimeter (top of 1), so G goes in.
explanation.definitionFit: Glanders is a serious contagious bacterial infection affecting mainly horses, mules and donkeys, causing nasal ulcers.

clue.text: Muslim scholars' rule may be disclosed

indicators.note: to disclose is to reveal what is already present, so the letters lie in plain view within the text

blocks.note: the letters run across the two words

explanation.surface: A dictum of Islamic jurists might be made public.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe makes 'scholars'' look possessive, but the plural noun alone is the definition and the rest hides the word.
explanation.definitionFit: The ulema are the body of learned religious authorities in Islam, trained in law and theology.

blocks.note: first word: to go away from or give up
second word defines SUIT, a set of clothes, the partner word one letter away

explanation.walkthrough: SUIT and QUIT differ in the first letter. S is already on the perimeter (foot of 13), and Q is otherwise missing, so QUIT is entered.
explanation.definitionFit: To quit is to depart from a place or job, or stop doing something altogether.

clue.text: Beast's owner gets a sovereign and a penny

blocks.note: a sovereign is a ruler, one who is lord over others
a copper is a low-value bronze coin such as a penny

explanation.surface: The owner of an animal is paid a gold coin and a penny.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beast' is not an animal but the Daily Beast, the newspaper in Evelyn Waugh's novel Scoop. A sovereign is also an old British gold coin, which keeps the money picture going.
explanation.definitionFit: In Waugh's satire Scoop, the pompous press baron who owns the Daily Beast newspaper is Lord Copper.

blocks.note: first word defines BILLOW, a large sea wave, the partner word one letter away
second word: a tree with long slender branches, often by water

explanation.walkthrough: BILLOW and WILLOW differ in the first letter; B is already on the perimeter (top of 3), so W is the one entered.
explanation.definitionFit: The willow is a deciduous tree or shrub of the genus Salix, typically growing near rivers.

clue.text: Connections with exchanges: see phone conversation — I shouldn't have said that!

blocks.note: lo, as in 'lo and behold', means look or see
a call is a conversation on the telephone
the exclamation after a slip of the tongue

explanation.surface: Someone discussing phone networks blurts out something indiscreet on a call and immediately regrets it.
explanation.walkthrough: The colon and dash make it look like a single remark, but the pieces simply run in order: a word for look, then the call, then the embarrassed exclamation.
explanation.definitionFit: In telephony, the local loop is the physical wire linking a subscriber's premises to the telephone exchange.

clue.text: One with lute, B playing — that would be B flat

indicators.note: musicians playing improvise and rework a tune, so these letters are rearranged too

blocks.note: taken as written
the instrument and the letter, taken as written

explanation.surface: A lutenist plays a B, and the clue remarks that the note sounds flat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'B flat' looks like a comment on poor playing, but it describes the answer: in blues and jazz in the key of C, the flattened seventh is B flat.
explanation.definitionFit: Blues and jazz bend certain scale degrees down a semitone; B flat is such a flattened note in the key of C.

blocks.note: first word defines THICKEN, as a sauce is reduced, the partner word one letter away
second word: a domestic fowl

explanation.walkthrough: THICKEN and CHICKEN differ only in the first letter. T is already on the perimeter (foot of 22 down), so C is needed.
explanation.definitionFit: The domestic fowl kept for eggs and meat is the commonest farmyard example of a bird.

clue.text: Spur to cuddle little helper at breakfast

blocks.note: to egg someone on is to urge or spur them
to spoon is to lie close and cuddle, curved together like stacked spoons

explanation.surface: A prompt to hug a small assistant at the breakfast table.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cuddle' seems a plain verb in the surface; it is the old slang sense of spoon, to court or snuggle up.
explanation.definitionFit: A small spoon used for eating boiled eggs from the shell is a modest utensil on the breakfast table.

indicators.note: nearly means not quite all, so the final letter is dropped

blocks.note: dementia, a decline of the mind, without its last letter

explanation.surface: Someone losing their faculties refuses to admit it.
explanation.walkthrough: The word is French, used in English for an official denial, especially in diplomacy.
explanation.definitionFit: A démenti is a formal, official contradiction of a rumour or report, typically issued by a government.

clue.text: Knight of romance on reported date with male

indicators.note: something reported is passed on by word of mouth, so it is heard rather than seen

blocks.note: a tryst is a lovers' secret date
a ram is a male sheep

explanation.surface: A tale of chivalry about a man's rumoured romantic meeting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Romance' sounds like love, fitting the date, but it means a medieval tale of chivalry.
explanation.definitionFit: Tristram, or Tristan, is the Arthurian knight whose doomed love for Isolde is told in medieval romances.

clue.text: Regretful agreement of doctor is a requirement

indicators.note: a requirement is something called for, so the letters are called on to take a fresh order

blocks.note: taken as written
Dr is the standard abbreviation for doctor
taken as written

explanation.surface: A doctor's reluctant yes, given because something is compulsory.
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram signal is loose here: 'requirement' has to be read as what the letters are put to. The answer is the colloquial clipped form of 'I'm afraid so'.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying 'fraid so' concedes that something unwelcome is true, an apologetic, sorry form of assent.

indicators.note: a word that does not reach its end loses its final letter

blocks.note: defines PILLAGER, the partner word one letter away; it adds nothing to the grid entry
vile, short of its last letter
a light, fizzy beer

explanation.surface: A buccaneer leaves an unpleasant pint half drunk.
explanation.walkthrough: This pair works differently: 'Pirate' defines PILLAGER, and the rest is wordplay for the partner, which has no definition of its own. P is already on the perimeter (top of 7), so V goes in.
explanation.definitionFit: The preamble's pairing stands in for a definition: this word is the one-letter partner of a raider, meaning a rural inhabitant.

clue.text: With marquetry feature, keeping quiet, being out of touch?

indicators.note: to keep something is to hold on to it, so one piece holds another

blocks.note: marquetry is decoration made of pieces of wood set into a surface
p is piano, the musical direction for soft

explanation.surface: A piece of furniture with inlaid wood, kept silent, seems detached from the world.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Out of touch' suggests being unaware, but in football or rugby 'touch' is the area beyond the sidelines; a ball not in touch is still live.
explanation.definitionFit: A ball that has not gone over the touchline remains live, so the game continues around it.

blocks.note: first word: a noun meaning an individual item or fact
second word defines DETAIN, to hold in custody, the partner word one letter away

explanation.walkthrough: 'Particular' is the noun here, as in 'in every particular'. N is already on the perimeter (foot of 16), so the L version is entered.
explanation.definitionFit: A particular, as a noun, is a single item or point of information, which is exactly a detail.

blocks.note: de is the French for 'of'
a Test is an international match in cricket or rugby

explanation.surface: Loathing of a foreign national team.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Of foreign' means the word for 'of' in a foreign language. A Test match is a full international fixture, chiefly in cricket.
explanation.definitionFit: To detest something is to dislike it intensely, a strong synonym of the verb hate.

blocks.note: going up
a tapering shape narrows to a point

explanation.surface: Something growing upward and narrowing, refusing the press baron.
explanation.walkthrough: In Waugh's Scoop, staff never contradict Lord Copper (11 across); when he is wrong they say 'Up to a point, Lord Copper', which really means no.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is the famously servile way Copper's employees disagree with him without ever uttering a flat refusal.

definitions.note: the answer is a place in Lorraine, not a phrase

blocks.note: first word defines METE, to measure out or allot, the partner word one letter away
second part: a city found in that French region

explanation.walkthrough: METE and METZ differ in the last letter; E is already on the perimeter (end of 14), and Z is needed, so the city goes in. Lorraine is a region of north-eastern France.
explanation.definitionFit: Metz is the historic capital city of the Lorraine region, on the Moselle river in north-eastern France.

blocks.note: first word defines MINE, the setter speaking of what belongs to me, the partner word one letter away
second word: an old-fashioned term for a cheeky person

explanation.walkthrough: In crosswords the setter refers to themself as 'me', so 'Setter's' is MINE. E is already on the perimeter, while X is needed, so MINX is entered.
explanation.definitionFit: A saucebox is a dated word for an impudent, cheeky person, especially a girl, which is what a minx is.

clue.text: Son of Welsh expert on test to see if wanted

blocks.note: ap is the Welsh patronymic meaning son of, as in ap Rhys
a pro is a professional, an expert

explanation.surface: A Welsh specialist's son is put on trial to see whether he is wanted.
explanation.walkthrough: Goods sent 'on appro' (short for approval) may be returned if the buyer does not want them; 'on' sits outside the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Appro is informal British shorthand for approval, a trial arrangement letting a customer try goods before buying.

clue.text: Southern states news: a horse given a girl's name

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for south or southern
the United States of America
N stands for new, doubled to make a plural, as pp stands for pages
taken as written
H is slang for heroin, itself known as horse

explanation.surface: A report from the American South: a horse has been named after a girl.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface recalls the Southern song 'Oh! Susanna'. Plurals of abbreviations are often doubled letters, hence two Ns; horse is drug slang for heroin.
explanation.definitionFit: Susannah is a common female first name of Hebrew origin, meaning lily, borne by a heroine of the Apocrypha.
